When I was a kid, I was interested in bikes and cars. I always wanted to figure out how things worked, or why they stopped working. I used to spend hours in my father’s garage repairing his old moped. I didn’t mind getting my hands dirty. When I was fifteen, I entered the Car and Road College in Bishkek. I decided to study Maintenance and Repair of Motor Vehicles.

While I was studying at college, I began working as a trainee in an auto service and repair shop. After I had been working for a year or two, I learned virtually every type of repair. This hands-on experience was really valuable. A good mechanic learns from doing, not reading.

Being a mechanic was not that easy. Repairing cars every day resulted in cuts and bruises and aches in places I didn’t even know existed! It was hard work, but I liked it. Every day brought some type of surprise or challenge. I loved the challenges because they were opportunities to learn. I also loved the feeling of fixing something that no one else could.

I’d been in the industry for about fifteen years when I decided to open my own auto service and repair shop. The first years were hard. With so much competition, I had to find creative ways of advertising to attract new customers. And of course, I had to find skilled mechanics – those who knew their job well.

Now, as I’ve been running my own shop for more than ten years, I can say that to be successful in any field, you need to be good at what you do and be willing to work hard.

2 Read or listen to Akyl’s conversation with his dad. Why is Akyl worried? What is he going to do?

Akyl: Morning!

Dad: You look worried. Is everything OK?

Akyl: Yes, I am fine. It’s just the lesson we had yesterday.

Dad: What lesson?

Akyl: Social studies. We talked about choosing a career and how important this decision is ...

Dad: I see. Well, it is an important decision, but you have plenty of time to think carefully, don’t you?

Akyl: I know, I know. But what if I make a bad choice and then I hate every single day of my life?

Dad: Calm down – you shouldn’t think that you will never be able to make changes in your life! After all, scholars predict that in the future people will frequently have to change their professions. Some professions will disappear because nobody will need them and some new ones will appear...

Akyl: I see. But I really don’t know where to start. How did you choose your profession?

Dad: Well, I always knew it would have to be related to cars. They were my passion since an early age. What are you interested in?

Akyl: Um, I like reading about animals and nature... Biology is my favourite subject at school. But I don’t think I want to become a biologist.

Dad: Hmm. There are lots of other jobs that require a good knowledge of biology: a health educator, a biochemist, a vet, a pharmacist, and many others. You just need to do some research about different professions, find out what people have to do in various jobs, what kind of skills and knowledge they need, and then think about yourself. Is it interesting to you? Do you have the abilities needed in this job? Will this profession be in demand in the future?

Akyl: I can’t answer the last question, but I can definitely learn about different professions and see which one suits me best! Well, thank you. Now, I know what to do.

cards.h: Language death: is it a real threat?

cards.h: Language death: is it a real threat?

cards.h: Language death: is it a real threat?

Chocolate chip cookies

It's hard to imagine a world without chocolate chip cookies, but the dessert wasn't actually invented until 1930. On the day they were created, Ruth Graves Wakefield was preparing some chocolate cookies for her guests when she realized that she was out of baker's chocolate. Thinking on her feet, Wakefield decided to chop up a block of Nestle semi-sweet chocolate, assuming that it would melt and spread evenly throughout the batter. Instead, what came out of the oven was chocolate chip cookies, a popular modern dessert.

Potato chips

One of the most popular snack foods, the potato chip, was invented in 1953 by George Crum, a chef at a restaurant in Saratoga Lake, New York, when one of his customers complained that their French-fried potatoes were not well cooked. As legend has it, potatoes were thinly sliced and fried until they were brown. The dish was loved by the customers and became the first-ever chips.

Ice-cream cones

Today, ice cream lovers have a choice between enjoying their treat in a cup or a cone, but that wasn't always the case. In 1904, Ernest A. Hamwi, the waffle vendor, thought that his waffles could be shaped into cones as vessels for the frozen ice-cream. In this way, he helped an ice cream vendor who ran out of dishes to serve his ice cream in.

Botox

In the 1980s, a new treatment for crossed eyes was being tested out in San Francisco. The ophthalmologist (eye doctor) noticed that his treatment had miraculous face-lifting side effects. Botox was invented as a result of the experiment.

Tea bags

The invention of the modern tea bag is credited to tea merchant Thomas Sullivan. In 1908, Sullivan began shipping samples of his tea out in small silk bags.Though his intention wasn't for people to use these as tea bags, customers did so anyway. The invention has been loved for its convenience.

Play-Doh

A popular toy among children all over the world, Play-Doh, was ironically created to be a cleaning product. The paste was first marketed in 1955 as a treatment for filthy wallpaper, but later it was used by schoolchildren to create arts and crafts projects.

Pieter Bruegel (1525–1569) is widely regarded as the 16th century's greatest Netherlandish painter. He is known for his landscapes and peasant scenes. Even in the 16th century, Habsburg collectors had recognised the exceptional quality and originality of Bruegel's imagery and bought his works. Bruegel's popularity is also a result of the stunning compositions he creates, which are often moralising and always teeming with characters, inviting the viewer to reflect on the multi-layered complexity of the image's contents. Paintings such as Proverbs, Children's Games, and The Wedding Dance are very recognisable and adored all over the world.

Hanging at the Gemaldegalerie art museum in Berlin, Germany, Netherlandish Proverbs is an unusual painting. Measuring 64 inches by 46 inches, this 16th century oil-on-oak-panel painting is populated by a swarm of miniature men, women, children, and animals performing a range of extraordinary and bizarre acts. However, most people who glance at Netherlandish Proverbs might see nothing more than a painting illustrating a bustling street scene in the Netherlands. Many of the actions performed by the subjects in the painting appear odd, but they all have meaning.

— When did you first know you would be an artist? When did you first start sculpting?

— I always knew I would be an artist. I was an artist before I was born. My earliest memory of myself is standing near my crib drawing on wallpaper with permanent markers. As soon as I was tall enough to reach the table, I carved into it with a kitchen knife. I grew up in a pre-computer, pre-smartphone, and pre-television environment; I played in mud, hung off tree limbs, made things out of whatever was on hand, and helped my dad to fix anything that needed repair. I didn't really think it necessary to decide on the kind of artist I would be, but when my parents gave me my first set of plasticine (modeling clay) for my 7th birthday, I knew I was a sculptor.

— What do sculptors do?

— A sculptor shapes clay, stone, marble, wood, and other materials (even ice and potatoes) into two- or three-dimensional art. To be a sculptor is to be a craftsman. I do everything myself, from start to finish: I mix my own clay, make metal armatures to support my clay sculptures, mold my finished pieces in flexible rubber with rigid plaster backing and cast waxes into the molds, and coat my waxes in heat-resistant ceramic. I pour bronze at 1177 °C into ceramic shells. I break ceramic off using a hammer.

I then cut, grind, refine, weld, and finish raw metal. I use chemicals and heat to change the color of raw bronze to one that suits a particular piece, which is a process called patination. I also fashion wood or marble bases for my finished sculptures. I drill, tap, and countersink in order for the sculpture to be mounted properly. I build my own pedestals — a lengthy, physical, and sweaty process that is also extremely satisfying because the result it yields is so personal.

— How would you describe your style of work?

— I am a contemporary sculptor reflecting on contemporary themes. I sculpt figures and animals in terra cotta and bronze. My sculptures communicate my ideas.

— Who or what inspires you artistically?

— I am a great admirer of nature. An artist's gift is two-fold: seeing the extraordinary in the ordinary and communicating that sense of wonder by way of art.

— Who are your clients?

— I create artwork to be used in a wide range of places, such as businesses, government buildings, homes, lawns, and outdoor parks, just to name a few.

— What is the hardest part of your job?

— Many sculptors work within tight deadlines, must also pay close attention to details, and work accurately, while always meeting the needs of the client.

— Do I have to study to become a sculptor?

— To become a sculptor, there is no specific educational requirement. I think I was born with an artistic talent, but I attended college to develop a skill set. At college, I had a chance to explore unfamiliar techniques, methods, and materials. I learned the history of sculpture through past and present artists. I developed sketching, molding, and casting techniques, and had the opportunity to participate in internships.

— And finally, sorry for the question, but I would like to know if it is a well-paid job.

— It's hard to say. When you first start working, you charge a nominal fee to earn a reputation, but after many years of professional experience you can command a much higher wage.

Indefinite article a/an

We use ‘a/an’ when ‘we don't know which one’, because the thing or person:

A. is one of many (He is a teacher. = there are many teachers)
B. is not unique (I have just bought a BMW.)
C. has not been mentioned before (There is a new student in our class.)

Definite article the

We use ‘the’ when ‘we know which one’, because the thing or person:

D. is unique or unique in that context (The Prime Minister of Kyrgyzstan has just resigned. = there is only one)
E. has been mentioned before (The student is very smart. = this student was mentioned before.)
F. is defined by the phrase which follows it. (What's the new student's name?)
G. with the superlative degree of adjectives (She is the most beautiful girl in my class.)

Zero article

We do not use an article when we talk about things in general:

H. using plural or uncountable nouns (Do you like mice?)
I. with the names of people or places (Akyl is my friend.)

Fixed phrases

We should learn by heart the following phrases:

J. a few, at home, at the beginning, at the end, go to bed, go to the cinema/theatre/station, in the world, once a week, sixty kilometers an hour, the next, the other, the other day, the same.

Other rules

K. With words like prison, university, church, mosque, school, hospital, etc., we use no article when we are thinking about the institution and the normal purpose we use it for: My sister had to stay at hospital for a few days. If we are thinking about the building, we use ‘the’. Our flat is opposite the hospital.

L. Phrases of time: the 25th of December / December the 25th, in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening (but at night, at lunchtime), the 1990s, the 21st century.

M. The names of most countries, continents, islands, states, provinces, towns, and cities do not use an article: in Asia, to Bishkek, from Texas, in Kazakhstan (exceptions are countries with the words Republic, Federation, Union, Confederation in the names: the Kyrgyz Republic, the Netherlands, the UK, the USA)

N. If we talk about a region we do not use an article: North-West India, North Europe, but in the east of the country, in the south of Italy, on the coast

1. Past simple and past continuous

The past simple shows complete, simple actions in the past — usually the main events in the story.

Every day brought some type of surprise or challenge.

The past continuous shows actions in progress at a time in the past. They often start before and continue after the main event of the story.

While I was studying at college, I began working as a trainee in an auto service and repair shop.

The past simple, not the past continuous, is usually used for verbs that describe states. These verbs include:

a) verbs that describe thought processes and opinions: agree, believe, forget, know, remember, think, etc.

b) verbs that describe emotions: hate, like, love, want, etc.

c) verbs that describe the five senses: feel, hear, see, smell, taste

d) others: be, have, belong, etc.

2. Past perfect simple and past perfect continuous

Both tenses describe events before the main events in the story.

Thepast perfect simple shows complete, simple actions or states before the main events in the story.

Before I finished school, I had decided to become a mechanic.

The past perfect continuous emphasises duration, and often shows actions that continue up until the main past events.

After I had been working for a year or two, I learned virtually every type of repair.

The past perfect simple, not the past perfect continuous, is usually used for verbs that describe states. See the list of state verbs in part 1.

UNIT 2

1. verb + to V1

These verbs don’t take an object before the to-infinitive (to V1): attempt, can’t afford, decide, hope, offer, plan, pretend, seem, try.

2. verb + sb + to V1

These verbs sometimes take an object before the to-infinitive (to V1): expect, help, promise, need, want, would like.

These verbs normally take an object before the to-infinitive (to V1): advise, allow, ask, teach, tell.

3. verb + sb + V1

These verbs take an object before the infinitive without to (V1): make and let.

4. verb + Ving

These verbs take the gerund (Ving): avoid, can’t stand, don’t mind, enjoy, finish, look forward to, spend time, suggest.

UNIT 3
Real conditionals

These sentences describe real situations. They consist of a main clause and an if-clause. The if-clause can come before the main clause or after the main clause. When it comes before the main clause, we use a comma.

If the weather is fine, we will go to the mountains.

We will go to the mountains if the weather is fine.

There are two types of real conditionals:

1. Zero conditional

These sentences describe what always happens in a particular situation. They are usually used to talk about facts or something that is always true.

If you heat water to 1000C, it boils. (scientific fact)

When I am tired, I always go to bed early. (This always happens in the same way.)

UNIT 4
Unreal conditionals

These sentences consist of an if-clause and a main clause. They are used to describe unreal / imaginary situations.

1. Second conditional

Second conditional is used to talk about dreams in the present / general time.

If + subject + past simple, subject + would + V1.

If I had a million dollars, I would travel around the world.

If people could speak to animals, they would become vegetarians.

Notice that in the if-clause, we can use were and was with I / he / she / it.

If I were / was a millionaire, I would travel around the world.

If my brother was / were not so lazy, he would study well at school.

We always use were when we give advice with If I were you.

If I were you, I would buy it. (Not If I was you, ...)

2. Third conditional

Third conditional is used to express regrets about past actions.

If + subject + past perfect, subject + would + have + V3.

If I hadn’t wasted so much money on stupid things, I would have gone to a café with my friends yesterday.

If I hadn’t borrowed some money from my friend, I wouldn’t have bought you a present.

2. Modals of deduction and for future possibility

We use the modal verbs might, may, and could + (not) V1 when we think it is (not) possible that something is true.

We use must when we are sure it is true and can’t when we are sure it isn’t true.

We use may/might and will to talk about things that are possible in the present and future.

UNIT 7
Modals of deduction

1. Modals of deduction (perfect modals)

Must and can’t / couldn’t + have + past participle is used when we are certain about situations in the past. Must and can’t are opposites:

I can’t find my keys. I must have left my keys at home.

May / might / could + have + past participle is used to talk about possibilities in the past (may have = possible, 50%; could / might have = less certain, 33%)

I am not sure what sort of bird it was that I saw yesterday, but it may/might/could have been an eagle.

Must / can / could / might / may + have + been + Ving is used when we are talking about certain or uncertain continuous actions in the past.

This man must have been living on the same street all his life. He knows everyone there.

2. Modals of deduction (deduction about present)

We use modals of possibility or probability + subject + be + Ving to make a guess or draw a logical conclusion about an activity in progress at the present time or during the time of speaking.

— What’s all that noise?

— The neighbour’s son must be listening to music.

Must conveys a strong feeling of certainty.

Could, may and might show that a speaker is 50% or less certain that an action is in progress.

Couldn’t and can’t show that the speaker believes strongly that a situation is not taking place.

May not and might not convey the idea that a speaker is 50% or less certain that an action is not possible or probable. They are not normally used in their contracted forms.

Articles

• Indefinite article ‘a / an’

We use ‘a / an’ when ‘we don’t know which one’, because the thing or person:

A. is one of many (He is a teacher. = there are many teachers)

B. is not unique (I have just bought a BMW.)

C. has not been mentioned before (There is a new student in our class.)

• Definite article ‘the’

We use ‘the’ when ‘we know which one’, because the thing or person:

D. is unique or unique in that context (The Prime Minister of Kyrgyzstan has just resigned. = there is only one)

E. has been mentioned before (The student is very smart. = this student was mentioned in example 3.)

F. is defined by the phrase that follows it (What’s the new student’s name?)

G. with the superlative degree of adjectives (She is the most beautiful girl in my class.)

• Zero article

We do not use an article when we talk about things in general:

H. using plural or uncountable nouns (Do you like mice?)

I. with the names of people or places (Akyl is my friend.)

• Fixed phrases

We should learn by heart the following phrases:

J. a few, at home, at the beginning, at the end, go to bed, go to the cinema / theatre / station, in the world, once a week, sixty kilometers an hour, the next, the other, the other day, the same.

• Other rules

K. With words like prison, university, church, mosque, school, hospital, etc., we use no article when we are thinking about the institution and the normal purpose we use it for: My sister had to stay at hospital for a few days. If we are thinking about the building, we use ‘the’. Our flat is opposite the hospital

L. Phrases of time: the 25th of December/December the 25th, in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening (but at night, at lunchtime), the 1990s, the 21st century

M. The names of most countries, continents, islands, states, provinces, towns, and cities do not use an article: in Asia, to Bishkek, from Texas, in Kazakhstan (exceptions are countries with the words Republic, Federation, Union, or Confederation in the names: the Kyrgyz Republic, the Netherlands, the UK, the USA)

N. If we talk about a region we do not use an article: North-West India, North Europe, but in the east of the country, in the south of Italy, on the coast

O. Most roads, streets, parks, bridges, shops, and restaurants do not use an article: Central Park, Baitik Batyr street, Tower Bridge

P. The names of theatres, cinemas, hotels, galleries, and museums use ‘the’: the Hermitage, the National Theatre, the Ala-Too cinema, the Hyatt

Q. The names of particular mountains and lakes do not take an article: Lake Issyk-Kul, Mount Korona; but if it is a group of mountains or islands, then we use article ‘the’: the Tian Shan mountains, the Galapagos Islands

R. Mountain ranges, groups of islands, rivers, seas, and canals use ‘the’: the Atlantic, the river Ak-Buura, the Ala-Too Mountains, the Big Chui Canal

S. Next and last with day, week, month, season, or year, in reference to the one directly after or before the current one, do not need any article.
